Chapter Two: How Power and Privilege Shape Everyday Life
There’s this moment that happens for a lot of us—maybe it’s in the office, or out shopping—when we suddenly realize the world isn’t quite as fair as we hoped. You know the feeling… You share an idea, but it only gets attention when someone else—someone who looks or sounds a little more like the people in charge—says it. Or maybe you notice you’re being watched more closely in a store, and you wonder why. Most of the time, these things get brushed off as misunderstandings. But if they keep happening, you start to see a pattern. And that’s when it hits: there’s something deeper going on.
Power in Britain doesn’t always show up with a title or a name tag. It’s tucked into the rules, the expectations, and all those unspoken agreements that guide our daily routines. For people who benefit from this power, it just feels normal—like this is the way things are supposed to be. But for anyone on the outside, it’s impossible not to notice the difference. Picture a young professional, eager to impress. They find that every mistake gets remembered, while their wins seem to fade away. Meanwhile, their colleagues—who share the same background as the folks in charge—get the benefit of the doubt. No one has to say anything out loud. The message is still crystal clear: some people just fit in better here.
That’s what privilege really looks like. Not just in big, obvious ways, but in all the small, daily moments where some people are given more space to fail, more chances to succeed, and more trust from those who make the rules. It’s the freedom to just live your life, without having to prove yourself at every turn.
A lot of people feel uncomfortable with the idea of privilege. It’s easier to believe everyone’s judged on their own merits, and that hard work is all you need to get ahead. But honestly, it’s never that simple. The systems that decide who lands a job, who gets believed, and who’s protected—they’ve been shaped by centuries of bias and exclusion.
Whenever the topic of race comes up, folks who benefit from privilege often get defensive. Maybe they say, “I don’t see color,” or “I’ve worked hard for everything I have.” That’s totally understandable. But here’s the thing: privilege isn’t about feeling guilty. It’s about recognizing the advantages that come from being part of a group that the system looks out for.
Imagine trying to explain what it feels like to always be on the outside. A friend gives it a shot, but every conversation ends the same way—with the other person insisting things aren’t really that bad, or that everyone faces challenges. That emotional effort—having to justify your own experience, again and again—it wears you down.
Most people don’t realize just how much energy it takes to move through a world that wasn’t built for you. The constant pressure to be twice as good, to watch every word, to avoid confirming stereotypes—it’s a weight that’s invisible to anyone who’s never had to carry it.
So, here’s the key takeaway: privilege isn’t an accusation. It’s a reality—and it’s something we have to acknowledge if we want real change. It’s not enough to just say, “I’m not racist.” The real goal is to be aware of how power works, and to use that awareness to make things fairer for everyone.
